entities.name: Weld-Blundell Prism
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Weld-Blundell Prism, dating to approximately 1820 BCE, is a significant artifact from ancient Mesopotamia, specifically linked to the Sumerian civilization. This prism, measuring about 30 cm tall and inscribed with an extensive royal list, chronicles the reigns of Sumerian kings, providing a critical timeline that aids in the understanding of early dynastic chronology. Its discovery at the site of Ur, one of the most influential city-states in ancient Sumer, underscores its importance in the historical narrative of early urban civilizations and their governance structures.

Inscribed on the prism are the names and reigns of various Sumerian rulers, presenting a historical record that connects political power to divine sanction, a common theme in Mesopotamian culture. The prism not only lists kings but also includes details about significant events and achievements during their reigns, such as military conquests and monumental constructions. It serves as a testament to the sophisticated administrative capabilities of the Sumerians and their emphasis on record-keeping as a means of legitimizing authority.

The legacy of the Weld-Blundell Prism extends beyond its immediate historical context, influencing later Mesopotamian scribes and historians who would look to its inscriptions as authoritative sources. Its existence has been pivotal in the study of Sumerian history, aiding scholars in reconstructing the timeline of ancient Mesopotamia and its cultural developments. The prism has been housed in various institutions, including the Ashmolean Museum, where it continues to be a vital resource for understanding the complexities of early state formations and historical narrative construction.
